Warm-up

Guess the next word

Your phone does this every time you type.

What comes next?

  1. Thank ______
  2. Happy ______
  3. I would like a cup of ______
  4. See you ______

Give them a minute, then take answers for each. 1 is almost always "you". 2 splits between birthday, new year, Diwali. 3 splits between tea and coffee. 4 splits between soon, later, tomorrow. That split is the point: the next word is a guess, and some guesses are surer than others.

How did you know?

  • You have read and heard these phrases thousands of times
  • After Thank, nearly always you: a very sure guess
  • After Happy: birthday, new year, Diwali…: several guesses, each with a chance
  • A computer can do the same: count what came next in a lot of text, and turn the counts into chances

A language model

A language model is a program that gives every possible next word a probability (a chance between 0 and 1).

You already use one

  • Your phone keyboard's suggestions
  • A search box that finishes your question
  • Chatbots, which write one guessed word at a time

The simplest language model: count which word comes after which.

By hand

Counting word pairs

Four tiny sentences

<s> i like tea </s>
<s> i like coffee </s>
<s> you like tea </s>
<s> i drink tea </s>
  • <s> and </s> are made-up words that mark the start and end of a sentence
  • With <s> we can guess the first word
  • With </s> we can guess when the sentence is finished

Idea 1: just count the words

word count
i 3
you 1
like 3
drink 1
tea 3
coffee 1
</s> 4
total 16

P(like) = 3 ÷ 16

We count the words that can come next, so </s> is counted and <s> is not: <s> is never a guess.

The problem with counting single words

  • This is a unigram model (uni = one): it looks at one word at a time
  • It ignores what you typed
  • Whatever you write, it suggests the same words

Idea 2: look at the word before

A bigram is a pair of neighbouring words (bi = two). We count them:

After… comes… count
<s> i 3
<s> you 1
i like 2
i drink 1
you like 1
After… comes… count
like tea 2
like coffee 1
drink tea 1
tea </s> 3
coffee </s> 1

From counts to a probability

After i, the next word was like 2 times out of 3.

P(like | i) = 2/3

Read it as "the probability of like, given i".

Exercise: next-word probabilities

<s> i like tea </s>
<s> i like coffee </s>
<s> you like tea </s>
<s> i drink tea </s>

(a) P(you | <s>)   (b) P(tea | like)   (c) P(tea | drink)   (d) P(</s> | tea)

(a) 1/4 (b) 2/3 (c) 1/1 = 1: drink was always followed by tea (d) 3/3 = 1

The probabilities after one word always add up to 1: P(tea | like) + P(coffee | like) = 2/3 + 1/3.

The probability of a whole sentence

A sentence is a chain of guesses. Multiply the steps, the way two heads in a row is ½ × ½ = ¼.

<s> i like tea </s>
<s> i like coffee </s>
<s> you like tea </s>
<s> i drink tea </s>
i like tea P(i | <s>) P(like | i) P(tea | like) P(</s> | tea)
3/4 2/3 2/3 3/3

3/4 × 2/3 × 2/3 × 1 = 1/3

Exercise: the probability of a sentence

<s> i like tea </s>
<s> i like coffee </s>
<s> you like tea </s>
<s> i drink tea </s>

(a) you like coffee    (b) you drink tea

(a) P(you | <s>) × P(like | you) × P(coffee | like) × P(</s> | coffee) = 1/4 × 1 × 1/3 × 1 = 1/12

(b) 1/4 × P(drink | you) × … = 1/4 × 0 × … = 0

Is "you drink tea" impossible?

  • "you like coffee" is not one of the four sentences, yet it gets 1/12: every pair in it was seen
  • "you drink tea" is good English too, yet it gets 0
  • Why?

The zero problem

you drink never appears in our four sentences, so P(drink | you) = 0. One zero makes the whole product 0.

  • The model confuses never seen with impossible
  • However much text you read, most word pairs never show up

Smoothing: add 1 to every count

Pretend you saw every pair once more, including the zeros. This is add-one smoothing:

\[ P_{\text{add-1}}(\text{next} \mid \text{word}) = \frac{\text{count(word next)} + 1}{\text{count(word)} + V} \]

V = how many different words can come next. Here V = 7: i, you, like, drink, tea, coffee, </s>.

Add-one smoothing after you

<s> i like tea </s>
<s> i like coffee </s>
<s> you like tea </s>
<s> i drink tea </s>
After you before add-one
like 1/1 2/8
drink 0 1/8
each of the other 5 0 1/8

No more zeros, and the seven still add up to 1: 2/8 + 6 × 1/8 = 8/8.

Exercise: add-one smoothing

<s> i like tea </s>
<s> i like coffee </s>
<s> you like tea </s>
<s> i drink tea </s>

V = 7.

(a) P(like | i)   (b) P(drink | i)   (c) P(i like tea): bigger or smaller than 1/3?

(a) (2 + 1) ÷ (3 + 7) = 3/10, down from 2/3   (b) (1 + 1) ÷ 10 = 2/10

(c) Smaller. Every pair we did see lost some probability, to pay for the pairs we didn't see.

Adding 1 can be too much

  • After i there are 3 real counts, and add-one hands out 7 made-up ones
  • So P(like | i) falls from 2/3 to 3/10: the real favourite is squashed
  • Real text has tens of thousands of words, so it is far worse

Add less: add-k smoothing

Add a small k (like 0.1) instead of 1:

\[ P_{\text{add-k}}(\text{next} \mid \text{word}) = \frac{\text{count(word next)} + k}{\text{count(word)} + k \cdot V} \]

Which k is best? We can't tell from the counts. We have to test.

How good is a model? Test it on new sentences

  • Training sentences: what the model counts (12 in the lab)
  • Test sentences: hidden from the model, used only to score it (4 in the lab)

Like a school exam: if the questions were the ones you practised, a high mark proves nothing.

On the training sentences every pair has been seen, so only new sentences show how the model copes.

Perplexity: how many words is it choosing between?

Before each word of a test sentence, the model gives the real next word a probability.

If every real word got… the model is as unsure as… perplexity
½ a coin toss 2
⅙ a dice roll 6
1/100 picking 1 of 100 words 100
1 someone who always knows 1

Lower is better. A good model is less surprised by real text.

The perplexity formula

\[ \text{Perplexity} = \sqrt[N]{\frac{1}{p_1 \times p_2 \times \cdots \times p_N}} \]

  • \( N \) = how many words the model had to guess in the test sentences (counting </s>)
  • \( p_i \) = the probability the model gave the real \( i \)-th word, e.g. P(tea | like)

Perplexity when the probabilities differ

Example: two words got ½ and ⅛, so \( N = 2 \), \( p_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} \), \( p_2 = \tfrac{1}{8} \).

\[ \text{Perplexity} = \sqrt[2]{\frac{1}{\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{8}}} \]

  1. Multiply them (the bottom of the fraction): ½ × ⅛ = 1/16
  2. Turn it upside down (the 1 over): 1 ÷ 1/16 = 16
  3. Take the \( N \)th root (square root for 2 words): √16 = 4

Formally, perplexity is 1 over the geometric mean of the probabilities. Avoid the term unless someone asks. In the lab, Python does it with (1 / product) ** (1 / N), where N is the number of probabilities.

Exercise: perplexity

(a) A model gives the three words of a test sentence the probabilities ½, ½ and ½. What is its perplexity?

(b) Another model gives two words ¼ and 1/16. What is its perplexity?

(c) Model A has perplexity 3 on the test sentences and model B has 10. Which would you put in the keyboard?

(a) Every word ½: 2   (b) ¼ × 1/16 = 1/64 → 64 → √64 = 8   (c) A: on average it is choosing between 3 words, B between 10.

Now in Python

words = ["<s>"] + sentence.split() + ["</s>"]   # mark start and end
pair_counts.update(zip(words, words[1:]))       # count every pair

next_counts("i")                                # {'like': 4, 'drink': 2}

def p_next(word, nxt):        # count of the pair ÷ count of the word
    after = next_counts(word)
    return after.get(nxt, 0) / sum(after.values())

W03-0, the pre-work notebook, has every one of these lines on the four tiny sentences. No data files, no pandas: just lists, Counter and loops.

Recap

  • From 12 sentences, the model suggests like → tea, coffee, hot, just from counting pairs
  • The probability of a sentence is every step multiplied together
  • "we like hot coffee" gets a probability although it isn't one of the 12: every pair was seen
  • "i drink cold tea" gets 0: nobody wrote drink cold. Never seen is not impossible
  • The model can write new sentences by gluing seen pairs together

Challenge lab

W03-B · Unseen word pairs, and scoring the model

A café app wants word suggestions in its order box.
Is our model good enough?

W03-B tasks

Task What you do
1 Find the test pairs the model has never seen
2 Add-one smoothing: no more zeros
3 Score the test sentences again
4 Perplexity: one number for the whole test
5 How much should we add? Try k = 1, 0.5, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001

The model learns from 12 sentences and is tested on 4 new ones. Every task checks itself.

Class discussion

What did you find?

Model, tested on 4 new sentences Perplexity
unigram: ignore the previous word 9.8
bigram, no smoothing can't compute: a zero
bigram, add-one 4.9
bigram, add-0.1 3.4

Four questions

  1. In plain words, what does "perplexity fell from 9.8 to 4.9" mean?
  2. Why could we not compute the perplexity of the bigram model with no smoothing?
  3. Adding 0.1 beat adding 1. Explain why, as you would to a friend.
  4. Our model read 12 sentences about tea and coffee. What would it suggest after "my doctor said"?

Q1: on average the model went from choosing between about 10 words (almost every word it knows) to about 5. Q2: "i drink cold tea" has two unseen pairs, so one probability is 0, the product is 0, and 1 ÷ 0 can't be done. Q3: add-one invents so many counts that the pairs we really saw lose too much probability; adding a little fixes the zeros without squashing the real favourites. Q4: nothing: it has never seen "my", "doctor" or "said". A model only knows the world of the text it read.

What the model learns from its text 🛑

Suppose the training text has "the doctor said he" 9 times and "the doctor said she" once.

The keyboard will suggest he after the doctor said, almost every time.

Three questions 🛑

  1. Nobody programmed that. Where did it come from?
  2. Millions of people see the same suggestions. Do they only copy how people write, or also change it?
  3. Search engines remove some suggestions about people and groups. Who should decide what goes?

Q1: from the training text: a language model copies the patterns, including the stereotypes, of whoever wrote it. Q2: both: suggestions are easy to accept, so common phrases get more common. Q3: no single right answer; the point is that someone has to look, because the model can't tell a stereotype from a fact.

The same counting, on 8 books

  • About 1 million words from 8 free classic novels: Pride and Prejudice, Sherlock Holmes, Dracula, …
  • It looks at the last 3 words, not just 1. A phrase it never saw? It drops the first word and tries again
  • Type a few words and it suggests the next one

Code: github.com/shripada/ngram-autocomplete

Demo: in the repo folder, uv run streamlit run app.py. Try "I do not" (know, think, mean), then "Sherlock" (holmes, every time), then "the purple elephant": nothing like it in the books, so it falls back to what follows "elephant". Move the n slider to 2 and 1 to show how much worse the guesses get with less context.

Where counting pairs stops working

"I bought it in March and by August it ___"

Looks only one word back: misses everything earlier → W9 transformers

tea · chai

Counts words, not meanings → W6 word vectors

"Not bad at all": good or bad?

The same counting idea, used to guess the feeling of a text → W4 sentiment

Short check

5 questions

Short check (1/2)

  1. Three tiny sentences: <s> the dog sleeps </s> · <s> the dog eats </s> · <s> the cat sleeps </s>.
    What is P(sleeps | dog)?
  2. Using the same three sentences, what is the probability of the sentence the cat eats? Explain your answer in one line.
  3. Use add-one smoothing on the same three sentences. The possible next words are the, dog, cat, sleeps, eats and </s>, so V = 6.
    (a) P(eats | cat)   (b) P(sleeps | cat)

Short check (2/2)

  1. A model gives every word of a test text a probability of 1/5. What is its perplexity, and what does that number mean?
  2. Model A has perplexity 120 on a set of test sentences, and model B has perplexity 300 on the same sentences. Which is better? Why must the test sentences be ones the models were not trained on?
